ui.title: Introduction
ui.answerFirst: Answer the question before going on.

pages.title: You are in command
body: You act as the incident commander at a wildfire. You do not fight the fire yourself; you follow the situation from the command post: the map, the units' reports and the drones' observations.

In each period you make a plan (an allocation): you choose the crews' main effort, i.e. the sector where most of the resources go, its posture, possibly a second sector with its task, and the drones' task.
No points are counted. What matters is that you build a picture of the situation and decide on it.

question.stem: What is the incident commander's main task?
options: Fighting the fire with a hose alongside the crew
Building a picture of the situation and deciding where the units concentrate
question.explanation: The commander neither fights the fire nor flies the drones. They gather information from the map and the reports and make the plan the units work by.

pages.title: Units and call signs
body: Every unit has a call sign it reports with. The letters tell where the unit is from: EK a unit of the own rescue department, KY of the neighbouring rescue department and OUT from outside the region. The number tells the units apart.

A rescue unit is a fire engine with its crew; 1+4 means a leader and four firefighters. A tanker carries a lot of water. A forest-fire unit has an off-road vehicle with hoses, portable pumps and basins. VOL is a volunteer fire brigade.
Drones (DR) film the fire from above, also with a thermal camera. A firefighting helicopter drops water from a bucket.
During the session, every call sign and unit type is on the Glossary & help card.

question.stem: Which of these call signs is a drone?
question.explanation: Call signs starting with DR are drones. Call signs starting with EK and KY are rescue department units.

pages.title: The shape of a fire and what drives it
body: A wildfire usually spreads into a long shape in the direction of the wind. The fastest-moving part is the head. Along its sides are the flanks, and at the back, on the upwind side, is the heel.
Wind, especially gusts, uphill slopes and dry ground speed a fire up. Dry litter and moss catch fire easily. If the fire rises into the tree crowns (a crown fire), it is fast and hot.
Dry peat, for example in a drained bog, can smoulder underground for a long time and flare up again. The wind can carry embers ahead of the fire, starting spot fires.

question.stem: The wind blows from west to east. In which direction does the head of a fire usually move?
question.explanation: The head usually moves with the wind. A wind from the west pushes the fire east, and the heel stays at the fire's western end.

pages.title: Anchoring and the flanks
body: A firefighting line is usually started where the fire cannot get round it: from a road, water or burnt ground. This is called anchoring.
A common way is to work from the anchor along the fire's flanks towards the head. At the head, flames are usually highest and the fire moves fastest.

The plan's postures are: direct attack (water or hand tools straight on the burning edge), a defensive line (the fire is stopped at a ready barrier such as a road or water) and protecting settlements (protecting buildings and people).

options: Starting a line where the fire cannot get round it
Parking all units in one place
Always stopping the head of the fire first
question.explanation: The anchor is the safe start of a line, e.g. a road, water or burnt ground. The line goes on from there, and the fire cannot get round its start.

pages.title: Water
body: Firefighting uses a lot of water. A rescue unit's own tank usually holds a few cubic metres, which lasts only a limited time on a hose line. Units report how many per cent of their tank is left.

More water is taken from water points (a lake, river or pond) with a portable pump, or brought by a tanker. A tanker drives between the water point and where the water is used: this is called a water shuttle or water run.
A tanker often empties its water into a basin set up in the field, from which a pump feeds the hose line. One round (filling, driving, emptying and returning) takes time.

question.stem: A tanker drives back and forth between a water point and the firefighting site. What is this called?
question.explanation: A water shuttle is carrying water with a tanker from a water point to where it is used and back. A hose line carries water from a pump to the fire, and mop-up is putting out smouldering spots after the fire.

pages.title: Safety
body: The crews' safety comes first. The memory aid LACES: Lookouts, Awareness, Communications, Escape routes and Safety zones.
An escape route is a route to safety agreed in advance. A safety zone is a place the fire does not threaten, e.g. burnt ground or a field. A lookout watches the fire and warns the crew.
A live power line is dangerous: no water is directed at the conductors, and no water is used near the line (within 15 metres) until the line has been switched off (de-energised).

options: The route a water shuttle takes
A route agreed in advance by which a crew can quickly reach safety
A road at which the fire is stopped
question.explanation: An escape route is the crew's safe way out: it is agreed in advance so that the crew can quickly reach safety if the fire threatens.

pages.title: The screen
body: In the middle is the map: the fire, the units and the sectors. The map legend at the bottom left tells what the symbols mean.
On the right are the message log, where the units' reports arrive, and the search tools. At the bottom you make your plan.
From time to time the situation is paused and the picture hidden. Answer the questions from memory then, and say how sure you are (scale 25–100).
To see what a word with a dotted underline means, point at it or tap it. The Glossary & help card has every word, unit and map symbol.

question.stem: Where do you see the units' reports?
question.explanation: The units' reports arrive in the message log on the right. The legend explains the map's symbols, and the plan is your decision.
